claim: Humans generate categories from complex regularities evolving across even imperfect sensory input.
source: Humans generate categories from complex regularities evolving across even imperfect sensory input.
evidence: This is a general statement about human cognition that draws from established scientific understanding.

claim: Incidental sound category learning emerged robustly when within-category sound exemplar variability was closely yoked to visuomotor task demands.
source: Incidental sound category learning emerged robustly when within-category sound exemplar variability was closely yoked to visuomotor task demands and was not apparent in the initial session when this coupling was less robust.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing Exp 2 and Exp 3 outcomes on Day-1.

claim: Incidental sound category learning was not apparent in the initial session when coupling of within-category exemplar variability to visuomotor task demands was less robust.
source: Incidental sound category learning emerged robustly when within-category sound exemplar variability was closely yoked to visuomotor task demands and was not apparent in the initial session when this coupling was less robust.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Exp 2 showing no significant RT Cost on Day-1.

claim: Incidentally acquired sound category knowledge was evident in both cases one day later.
source: Nonetheless, incidentally acquired sound category knowledge was evident in both cases one day later, indicative of offline learning gains
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing RT Costs on Day-2 in both Exp 2 and Exp 3.

claim: Offline learning gains occurred in incidental sound category learning.
source: Nonetheless, incidentally acquired sound category knowledge was evident in both cases one day later, indicative of offline learning gains
evidence: This claim is inferred from the emergence of RT Costs on Day-2 that were not present (Exp 2) or equivalent (Exp 3) on Day-1.

claim: Learning in both cases supported explicit category labeling of novel sounds nine days later.
source: and, nine days later, learning in both cases supported explicit category labeling of novel sounds.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the Day-10 explicit labeling task showing above-chance performance.

claim: A relatively brief incidental experience with multi-dimensional sound patterns aligned with behaviorally relevant actions and events can generate new sound categories.
source: Thus, a relatively brief incidental experience with multi-dimensional sound patterns aligned with behaviorally relevant actions and events can generate new sound categories, immediately after the learning experience or a day later.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing RT Costs and generalization performance across experiments.

claim: Incidentally learned categories undergo consolidation into long-term memory to support robust generalization of learning.
source: These categories undergo consolidation into long-term memory to support robust generalization of learning, rather than simply reflecting recall of specific sound-pattern exemplars previously encountered.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing maintained RT Costs and above-chance generalization to novel exemplars on Day-10.

claim: Incidentally learned categories do not simply reflect recall of specific sound-pattern exemplars previously encountered.
source: These categories undergo consolidation into long-term memory to support robust generalization of learning, rather than simply reflecting recall of specific sound-pattern exemplars previously encountered.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing generalization to novel exemplars not experienced during training.

claim: Humans forage for information to acquire and consolidate new knowledge that may incidentally support behavior, even when learning is not strictly necessary for performance.
source: Humans thus forage for information to acquire and consolidate new knowledge that may incidentally support behavior, even when learning is not strictly necessary for performance.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental findings showing incidental learning in a task where sounds were not necessary for performance.

claim: Edible mushrooms may tend to have a typical shape, or smell, or color but none of these cues, on its own, may be entirely diagnostic of a safe meal.
source: For example, edible mushrooms may tend to have a typical shape, or smell, or color but none of these cues, on its own, may be entirely diagnostic of a safe meal.
evidence: This is an illustrative example drawing on general knowledge about mushroom identification.

claim: To generate categories, imperfect and complex regularities present in the sensory input must be extracted and learned.
source: To generate categories, imperfect and complex regularities present in the sensory input must be extracted and learned, but this knowledge then needs to be consolidated into long-term memory to be called upon to guide behavior when encountering novel objects and events with similar properties.
evidence: This is a general statement about category learning that draws from established scientific understanding.

claim: Category knowledge needs to be consolidated into long-term memory to be called upon to guide behavior when encountering novel objects and events with similar properties.
source: To generate categories, imperfect and complex regularities present in the sensory input must be extracted and learned, but this knowledge then needs to be consolidated into long-term memory to be called upon to guide behavior when encountering novel objects and events with similar properties.
evidence: This is a general statement about memory consolidation that draws from established scientific understanding.

claim: Most studies have examined category learning under conditions in which learners overtly direct attention to explicit category decisions and receive feedback about the correctness of their decisions.
source: Yet, most studies have examined category learning under conditions in which learners overtly direct attention to explicit category decisions and receive feedback about the correctness of their decisions (Holt and Lotto, 2006; Goudbeek et al., 2009; Guenther et al., 1999; Holt et al., 2004; Mirman et al., 2004; Earle and Myers, 2015; Earle et al., 2017; Ashby and Maddox, 2005; Love, 2002; Love et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research in the field.

claim: Category learning can proceed even under incidental conditions when the regularities underlying sensory input categories align with successful behavior on a primary task ostensibly unrelated to a need for categorization.
source: However, there is ample evidence that category learning can proceed even under incidental conditions when the regularities underlying sensory input categories align with successful behavior on a primary task ostensibly unrelated to a need for categorization.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and the current experimental findings.

claim: Adult listeners are capable of generating multidimensional auditory categories when auditory categories incidentally align with successful behavior in a visuomotor task.
source: Adult listeners are capable of generating multidimensional auditory (Gabay et al., 2015; Leech et al., 2009; Lim and Holt, 2011; Roark and Holt, 2018; Wade and Holt, 2005; Roark et al., 2022) and phonetic speech (Lim and Holt, 2011; Lim et al., 2015) categories when auditory categories incidentally align with successful behavior in a visuomotor task (i.e. when the task can be completed without recourse to the auditory input).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Adult listeners are capable of generating phonetic speech categories when auditory categories incidentally align with successful behavior in a visuomotor task.
source: Adult listeners are capable of generating multidimensional auditory (Gabay et al., 2015; Leech et al., 2009; Lim and Holt, 2011; Roark and Holt, 2018; Wade and Holt, 2005; Roark et al., 2022) and phonetic speech (Lim and Holt, 2011; Lim et al., 2015) categories when auditory categories incidentally align with successful behavior in a visuomotor task (i.e. when the task can be completed without recourse to the auditory input).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Incidentally acquired auditory category knowledge can generalize to encompass novel category exemplars.
source: Moreover, this incidentally acquired auditory category knowledge can generalize to encompass novel category exemplars and has been shown to draw on cortical and cortico-striatal networks associated with speech-related category expertise (Leech et al., 2009; Liu and Holt, 2011; Lim et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and the current experimental findings.

claim: Incidentally acquired auditory category knowledge draws on cortical and cortico-striatal networks associated with speech-related category expertise.
source: Moreover, this incidentally acquired auditory category knowledge can generalize to encompass novel category exemplars and has been shown to draw on cortical and cortico-striatal networks associated with speech-related category expertise (Leech et al., 2009; Liu and Holt, 2011; Lim et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Incidental auditory category learning draws upon internal feedback associated with success in the primary task.
source: this supports the notion that incidental auditory category learning draws upon internal feedback associated with success in the primary task (Lim et al., 2019; Roark et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Response time to detect the visual target was stable across the first 8 blocks of training on Day-1 in Exp 1.
source: Response time (RT) to detect the target was stable across the first 8 blocks of training on Day-1 [F (7, 147)=0.76, p=0.61; ηp²=0.03; Figure 2A], indicating no significant task-driven online learning on Day-1.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and reference to Figure 2A.

claim: There was no significant task-driven online learning on Day-1 in Exp 1.
source: Response time (RT) to detect the target was stable across the first 8 blocks of training on Day-1 [F (7, 147)=0.76, p=0.61; ηp²=0.03; Figure 2A], indicating no significant task-driven online learning on Day-1.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the statistical analysis showing stable RT across blocks.

claim: RT to respond to the visual target in the first block of Day-2 was significantly faster compared to the final block of Day-1 in Exp 1.
source: However, RT to respond to the visual target in the first block of Day-2 (Block 9, M=437.8ms, SE = 11.2ms) was significantly faster compared to the final block of Day-1 (Block 8, M=481.4ms, SE = 14.2ms), indicative of offline learning gains in visuomotor task performance [t(21)=–3.83, p=0.001, Cohen's d=–0.81].
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Offline learning gains in visuomotor task performance occurred between Day-1 and Day-2 in Exp 1.
source: However, RT to respond to the visual target in the first block of Day-2 (Block 9, M=437.8ms, SE = 11.2ms) was significantly faster compared to the final block of Day-1 (Block 8, M=481.4ms, SE = 14.2ms), indicative of offline learning gains in visuomotor task performance [t(21)=–3.83, p=0.001, Cohen's d=–0.81].
evidence: This claim is inferred from the significant RT difference between sessions.

claim: The facilitation in the speed of reporting the visual target did not come at a cost to accuracy in Exp 1.
source: This facilitation in the speed of reporting the visual target did not come at a cost to accuracy (see Appendix 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Appendix 1.

claim: The RT facilitation was robustly maintained across a 9-day interval in Exp 1.
source: and, moreover, was robustly maintained across a 9-day interval [final block of Day-2, M=449.29ms, SE = 12.06ms, to the first block of Day-10, M=437.15ms, SE = 11.32ms; t(1,)=–1.79, p=0.08; Cohen's d=-0.38].
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant difference between Day-2 and Day-10.

claim: There was no significant RT Cost for Block 7 in Exp 2, indicating no robust incidental learning after the 6 practice blocks.
source: There was no significant RT Cost for Block 7 wherein the category-to-location association was disrupted in Exp 2, indicating no robust incidental learning after the 6 practice blocks [t(23)=0.43, p=0.66, Cohen's d=0.08, MBlock7=466.1ms, SEBlock7=13.8ms; MBlock6=461.9ms, SEBlock6=17.28ms].
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Exp 3, there was a significant RT Cost indicative of incidental category learning on Day-1.
source: In Exp 3, in which participants experienced within-category variability on each visuomotor trial, there was a significant RT Cost indicative of incidental category learning on Day-1 [t(21)=2.77, p=0.01, Cohen's d=.59, MBlock7=446.06ms, SEBlock7=16.28ms; MBlock6=409.41ms, SEBlock6=19.13ms].
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Incidental auditory category learning in Exp 3 was reflected as a decrease in RT across Blocks 1–6.
source: Incidental auditory category learning in Exp 3 was also reflected as a decrease in RT across Blocks 1–6 conveying the category-to-location association [F(5, 105)=2.87, p=0.01, ηp²=.12].
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Response time was facilitated in Blocks 4–6 compared to the earlier Blocks 1–3 in Exp 3.
source: Response time was facilitated in Blocks 4–6 (MBlocks4-6 = 407.6 ms, SEBlocks4-6 = 20.3 ms) compared to the earlier Blocks 1–3 (M Blocks1-3 = 424.5 ms, SEBlocks1-3 = 17.9 ms) [F (1, 21)=7.19, p=0.01; ηp²=0.25].
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The speeding of RT in Exp 3 was not at the cost of accuracy.
source: This speeding of RT was not at the cost of accuracy (see Appendix 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Appendix 1.

claim: The RT facilitation across Exp 3 Blocks 1–6 is unlikely to have been driven by visuomotor task practice and learning.
source: This facilitation of RT is unlikely to have been driven by visuomotor task practice and learning as it was not observed in Exp 1, [F (5, 105)=0.99, p=0.42; ηp²=0.04] or in Exp 2 [F(5, 115)=0.30, p=0.91; ηp²=0.01], in which incidental category learning was not evident as an RT Cost.
evidence: This claim is inferred from comparison of RT patterns across experiments.

claim: The RT facilitation across Exp 3 Blocks 1–6 can be ascribed, at least in part, to within-session incidental learning of the auditory categories.
source: Thus, the RT facilitation across Exp 3 Blocks 1–6 can be ascribed, at least in part, to within-session incidental learning of the auditory categories.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the pattern of results across experiments.

claim: Single-session category learning was more robust when multiple exemplars of the same category preceded each trial's visuomotor target (Exp 3) than when a single exemplar was repeatedly presented before the target (Exp 2).
source: Single-session category learning was more robust when multiple exemplars of the same category preceded each trial's visuomotor target (Exp 3) than when a single exemplar was repeatedly presented before the target and thus exemplar variability was experienced only across trials (Exp 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of RT Cost data between Exp 2 and Exp 3 on Day-1.

claim: Per-trial many-to-one auditory-to-visuomotor correspondence serves as a 'representational glue' to bind together acoustically distinct sound exemplars to enhance incidental category learning compared to cross-trial binding.
source: This differential pattern of results is consistent with the notion of per-trial many-to-one auditory-to-visuomotor correspondence serving as a 'representational glue' to (better) bind together acoustically distinct sound exemplars to enhance incidental category learning compared to cross-trial binding.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the differential learning outcomes between Exp 2 and Exp 3.

claim: A significant RT Cost emerged by Day-2 of Exp 2, indicative of incidental auditory category learning.
source: A significant RT Cost emerged by Day-2 of Exp 2, indicative of incidental auditory category learning [t(23)=2.78, p=0.01; Cohen's d=0.56].
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Disrupting the category-to-location association in Block 10 led to slower visuomotor responses than in the preceding Block 9 in Exp 2.
source: Disrupting the category-to-location association in Block 10 led to slower visuomotor responses (MBlock10=449.13ms, SEBlock10=14.79ms) than in the preceding Block 9 in which the association was present (MBlock9=426.7ms, SEBlock9=17.2ms).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: A Day-2 RT Cost was evident in Exp 3.
source: Similarly, a Day-2 RT Cost was evident in Exp 3 [t(21)=2.18, p=0.04; Cohen's d=0.46], with slower visuomotor responses upon disruption of the category-to-location association (MBlocks10=415.01ms, S.E.Blocks10=12.58ms) compared to the preceding block (MBlocks9=385.35ms, S.E.Blocks9=18.33ms).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The magnitude of the RT Cost was as large on Day-2 as on Day-1 in Exp 3.
source: Here, the magnitude of the RT Cost was as large on Day-2 as on Day-1 [t(21)=0.64, p=0.52; Cohen's d=0.11; Figure 2C] indicating maintenance, but not further evolution, of incidental category learning across sessions.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 2C.

claim: There was maintenance, but not further evolution, of incidental category learning across sessions in Exp 3.
source: Here, the magnitude of the RT Cost was as large on Day-2 as on Day-1 [t(21)=0.64, p=0.52; Cohen's d=0.11; Figure 2C] indicating maintenance, but not further evolution, of incidental category learning across sessions.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the statistical analysis showing no significant difference in RT Cost between Day-1 and Day-2.

claim: There were offline gains in the speed of visuomotor task responses from the last block of Day-1 to the first block of Day-2 in Exp 2.
source: There also were offline gains in the speed of visuomotor task responses, expressed as a facilitation in RT from the last block of Day-1 to the first block of Day-2, that were apparent in both Exp 2 [t(1, 23)=–2.15, p=0.04; Cohen's d=–0.42]
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: There were offline gains in the speed of visuomotor task responses from the last block of Day-1 to the first block of Day-2 in Exp 3.
source: There also were offline gains in the speed of visuomotor task responses, expressed as a facilitation in RT from the last block of Day-1 to the first block of Day-2, that were apparent in both Exp 2 [t(1, 23)=–2.15, p=0.04; Cohen's d=–0.42] and Exp 3 [t(1, 21)=–2.35, p=0.028; Cohen's d=–0.5], with faster responses to the visual target on the first block of Day-2 than the last block of Day-1 (mean difference 17.7ms Exp 2, 37.4ms Exp 3; Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and reference to Figure 2.

claim: The delayed gains in speed were not at the cost of accuracy in Exp 2 and Exp 3.
source: These delayed gains in speed were not at the cost of accuracy [see Appendix 1—figure 1 and Appendix 1].
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Appendix 1.

claim: The offline gains observed in Exp 2 and Exp 3 are most likely attributable to visuomotor learning.
source: In view of the robust offline gains observed in Exp 1 when no sounds were present, these gains are most likely to be attributable to visuomotor learning, but there is the possibility of concurrent benefits from category learning.
evidence: This claim is inferred from comparison with Exp 1 results.

claim: There is the possibility of concurrent benefits from category learning contributing to offline gains in Exp 2 and Exp 3.
source: In view of the robust offline gains observed in Exp 1 when no sounds were present, these gains are most likely to be attributable to visuomotor learning, but there is the possibility of concurrent benefits from category learning.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential contributions to offline gains.

claim: The RTs of the first and last halves of Block 8 did not differ significantly in Exp 2.
source: For Exp 2, the RTs of the first and last halves of Block 8 did not differ significantly [t(46)=–0.204, p=0.839, Cohen's d=0.005]
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: There was no significant RT difference between Blocks 6 and 8 in Exp 2.
source: and there was no significant RT difference between Blocks 6 and 8 [t(46)=–0.717, p=0.476, Cohen's d=0.207].
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: RTs in the first and second halves of Block 8 did not differ in Exp 3.
source: The same held for Exp 3: RTs in the first and second halves of Block 8 did not differ [t(44)=0.340, p=0.735, Cohen's d=0.100]
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: RTs did not differ between Blocks 6 and 8 in Exp 3.
source: nor did they differ between Blocks 6 and 8 [t(42)=–0.480, p=0.633, Cohen's d=0.14].
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: There was no evidence of interference by Block 7 in Exp 2 and Exp 3.
source: In all, there was no evidence of interference by Block 7, or of a loss of performance from Blocks 6–8 that could explain the observed offline gains.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the statistical analyses showing no RT differences.

claim: There was no loss of performance from Blocks 6–8 that could explain the observed offline gains in Exp 2 and Exp 3.
source: In all, there was no evidence of interference by Block 7, or of a loss of performance from Blocks 6–8 that could explain the observed offline gains.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the statistical analyses showing no RT differences.

claim: There was no difference in the magnitude of RT Cost in the blocks preceding versus following a 3-hour daytime break in the control experiment.
source: There was no difference in the magnitude of RT Cost in the blocks preceding versus following the break [t(20)=–1.10, p=0.28; Cohen's d=0.26].
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of control experiment data.

claim: The offline gains in auditory category knowledge observed in Exp 2 are unlikely to be attributable to practice from Day-2 Block 9.
source: Thus, we conclude that the offline gains in auditory category knowledge observed in Exp 2 are unlikely to be attributable to practice from Day-2 Block 9, and instead point to offline gains.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the control experiment results showing no difference across a daytime break.

claim: There were significant RT Costs on Day-10 in Exp 2.
source: There were significant RT Costs on Day-10 in Exp 2 [t(23)=2.76, p=0.01; Cohen's d=0.56; Figure 2B]
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 2B.

claim: There were significant RT Costs on Day-10 in Exp 3.
source: There were significant RT Costs on Day-10 in Exp 2 [t(23)=2.76, p=0.01; Cohen's d=0.56; Figure 2B] and Exp 3 [t(21)=2.25 p=0.03; Cohen's d=0.47; Figure 2C]
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 2C.

claim: The magnitude of the RT Costs on Day-10 were as large as those attained on Day-2 in Exp 2.
source: and, moreover, the magnitude of the RT Costs on Day-10 were as large as those attained on Day-2 in both Exp 2 [t(23)=–0.62, p=0.54; Cohen's d=0.08]
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The magnitude of the RT Costs on Day-10 were as large as those attained on Day-2 in Exp 3.
source: and, moreover, the magnitude of the RT Costs on Day-10 were as large as those attained on Day-2 in both Exp 2 [t(23)=–0.62, p=0.54; Cohen's d=0.08] and Exp 3 [t(21)=0.20, p=0.83; Cohen's d=0.03].
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Exp 2, participants' RT Costs on Day-1 and Day-2 were significantly correlated.
source: In Exp 2, participants' RT Costs on Day-1 and Day-2 were significantly correlated (r=0.737, p=0.001)
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Exp 2, the RT Costs incurred on Day-2 and Day-10 were significantly correlated.
source: as were the RT Costs incurred on Day-2 and Day-10 (r=0.778, p=0.001)
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Exp 2, Day-1 and Day-10 RT Costs were significantly correlated.
source: and Day-1 and Day-10 (r=0.571, p=0.004).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Exp 3, there were significant correlations between participants' RT costs incurred on Day-1 and Day-2.
source: The same pattern was found in Exp 3, with significant correlations between participants' RT costs incurred on Day-1 and Day 2- (r=0.670, p=0.001)
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Exp 3, Day-2 and Day-10 RT Costs were significantly correlated.
source: as well as Day-2 and Day-10 RT Costs (r=0.730, p=0.001)
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Exp 3, Day-1 and Day-10 RT Costs were significantly correlated.
source: and Day-1 and Day-10 (r=0.614, p=0.002).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of experimental data.

claim: Category knowledge generalized to support placing novel sounds in the appropriate location associated with its category at above-chance levels in Exp 2 for unidimensional categories.
source: Category knowledge generalized to support placing novel sounds in the appropriate location associated with its category at above-chance levels in Exp 2 for both category types (Figure 1A) [unidimensional categories: t(23) = 2.89, p=0.008; Cohen's d=0.57
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Category knowledge generalized to support placing novel sounds in the appropriate location associated with its category at above-chance levels in Exp 2 for multidimensional categories.
source: Category knowledge generalized to support placing novel sounds in the appropriate location associated with its category at above-chance levels in Exp 2 for both category types (Figure 1A) [unidimensional categories: t(23) = 2.89, p=0.008; Cohen's d=0.57; multidimensional: t(23) = 3.104, p=0.005; Cohen's d=0.60].
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Categorization performance in Exp 2 was not dependent on whether the category was defined by a unidimensional acoustic cue or by more complex, multidimensional, acoustic regularities.
source: Categorization performance was not dependent on whether the category was defined by a unidimensional acoustic cue (rising vs. falling frequency of one component of the complex sound) or by more complex, multidimensional, acoustic regularities, [t(23)=0.73, p=0.47; Cohen's d=0.07] (Wade and Holt, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and citation to prior research.

claim: Category knowledge generalized to novel sounds in Exp 3 for unidimensional categories.
source: Category knowledge also generalized to novel sounds in Exp 3 [unidimensional: t(21) = 3.77, p=0.001; Cohen's d=0.78
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Category knowledge generalized to novel sounds in Exp 3 for multidimensional categories.
source: Category knowledge also generalized to novel sounds in Exp 3 [unidimensional: t(21) = 3.77, p=0.001; Cohen's d=0.78, multidimensional: t(21) = 2.52, p=0.01; Cohen's d=0.53]
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Performance in the unidimensional categories was more accurate compared to multidimensional categories in Exp 3.
source: although here performance in the unidimensional categories was more accurate compared to multidimensional categories [t(21)=.3.11, p=0.005; Cohen's d=0.37].
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Overall, generalization to novel exemplars did not differ across Exp 2 and Exp 3.
source: We also compared generalization to novel exemplars across Exp 2 and Exp 3. Overall, generalization to novel exemplars did not differ across experiments, [t(44)=0.54, p=0.58; Cohen's d=0.18].
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis comparing experiments.

claim: In both Exp 2 and Exp 3, the magnitude of a participant's RT Cost on Day-1, Day-2, and Day-10 was highly predictive of the accuracy of category generalization in an explicit category labeling task on Day-10.
source: In both Exp 2 and Exp 3, the magnitude of a participant's RT Cost on Day-1, Day-2, and Day-10 was highly predictive of the accuracy of category generalization in an explicit category labeling task on Day-10 (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analyses and reference to Figure 3.

claim: In Exp 2, the high-performing subgroup had a tendency to exhibit greater RT Costs compared to the low-performing subgroup on Day-2.
source: Thus, a median split of participants based on their explicit labeling accuracy on Day-10 into two subgroups, high-performing and low-performing showed, in Exp 2, that the high-performing subgroup had a tendency to exhibit greater RT Costs, compared to the low-performing subgroup, on Day-2 [t(22)=–1.79, p=0.08, Cohen's d=–0.733]
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of subgroup data.

claim: In Exp 2, the high-performing subgroup exhibited greater RT Costs than the low-performing subgroup on Day-10.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of subgroup data.

claim: In Exp 2, the high-performing and low-performing subgroups did not differ in RT Cost on Day-1.
source: although the subgroups did not differ on Day-1, t(22) = –1.30, p=0.21, Cohen's d=–0.533.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of subgroup data.

claim: In Exp 3, the high-performing subgroup exhibited significantly greater RT Costs than the low-performing subgroup on Day-2.
source: In Exp 3, the high-performing subgroup exhibited significantly greater RT Costs than the low-performing subgroup on Day-2 [t (20)=–3.82, p=0.001; Cohen's d=–0.721]
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of subgroup data.

claim: In Exp 3, the high-performing subgroup exhibited significantly greater RT Costs than the low-performing subgroup on Day-10.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of subgroup data.

claim: In Exp 3, the high-performing and low-performing subgroups' RT Costs did not differ on Day-1.
source: although, here too, the subgroups' RT Costs did not differ on Day-1 [t(20)=–1.69, p=0.106; Cohen's d=-0.721].
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of subgroup data.

claim: The overnight, offline gains in SMART performance were not predictive of the ability to categorize novel stimuli accurately on Day-10.
source: However, the overnight, offline gains in SMART performance (the facilitation in RT between sessions) were not predictive of the ability to categorize novel stimuli accurately on Day-10 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analyses and reference to Figure 3C.

claim: The lack of a relationship between overnight gains and category generalization argues that skill consolidation in the visuomotor task is likely to be the primary driver of overnight RT facilitation.
source: Together with the results of Exp 1 demonstrating robust overnight gains with no sounds, the lack of a relationship between overnight gains and category generalization argues that skill consolidation in the visuomotor task is likely to be the primary driver of overnight RT facilitation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the pattern of results across experiments.

claim: Two contemporaneous learning processes – visuomotor task learning and incidental category learning – are evident in the present results.
source: This, in turn, suggests that two contemporaneous learning processes – visuomotor task learning and incidental category learning – are evident in the present results.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the dissociation between offline gains and category generalization.

claim: After a relatively brief experience practicing a simple visuomotor task in which acoustic input is unnecessary for task performance, young adults learn about auditory category structure of the sounds and use it to hone visuomotor response.
source: After a relatively brief experience practicing a simple visuomotor task in which acoustic input is unnecessary for task performance, young adults learn about auditory category structure of the sounds and use it to hone visuomotor response.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental findings showing RT Costs.

claim: Learning extends beyond simple auditory-to-visuomotor mappings because it generalizes to support categorization of sounds not previously encountered.
source: This learning extends beyond simple auditory-to-visuomotor mappings because it generalizes to support categorization of sounds not previously encountered.
evidence: This claim is supported by the generalization data from the explicit labeling task.

claim: Participants process repeated information and establish new knowledge to support behavior, even when it is not strictly necessary.
source: Participants thus process repeated information and establish new knowledge to support behavior, even when it is not strictly necessary – as in the SMART, a simple visuomotor task that can be completed with high accuracy without any reliance on the sounds.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental findings showing incidental learning despite sounds being unnecessary.

claim: Category knowledge emerging from incidental experience is further elaborated and consolidated into long-term memory after the termination of the initial session.
source: The current results underscore an important outcome of the SMART training experience: category knowledge emerging from incidental experience is further elaborated and consolidated into long-term memory after the termination of the initial session.
evidence: This claim is supported by the emergence of RT Costs on Day-2 and their maintenance on Day-10.

claim: There was evidence for robust within-session, 'online', auditory category learning in Exp 3.
source: There was evidence for robust within-session, 'online', auditory category learning in Exp 3
evidence: This claim is supported by the significant RT Cost on Day-1 in Exp 3.

claim: There was no clear-cut evidence for auditory category learning during the first session of Exp 2.
source: however, there was no clear-cut evidence for auditory category learning during the first session of Exp 2.
evidence: This claim is supported by the lack of significant RT Cost on Day-1 in Exp 2.

claim: By the second session of Exp 2 learners' performance became significantly reliant on the availability of the sound categories.
source: Nevertheless, by the second session of Exp 2 learners' performance became significantly reliant on the availability of the sound categories, indicating that auditory category learning had occurred
evidence: This claim is supported by the significant RT Cost on Day-2 in Exp 2.

claim: Nine days later, generalization of category knowledge in Exp 2 was as robust as that of learners in Exp 3.
source: and, nine days later, their generalization of category knowledge was as robust as that of learners in Exp 3.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison of explicit labeling accuracy between experiments.

claim: Gains reflecting the setting up and utilization of the new sound categories occur post-session and can be expressed as 'offline' gains after the training experience has ended.
source: Therefore, in addition to performance gains that can be observed as 'online learning' within a single training session, gains reflecting the setting up and utilization of the new sound categories occur post-session and can be expressed as 'offline' gains after the training experience has ended (Karni and Sagi, 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental findings and citation to prior research on offline gains.

claim: Delayed gains emerging in the post learning interval are believed to reflect memory consolidation.
source: These latter, delayed gains emerging in the post learning interval are believed to reflect memory consolidation—the process by which memories become less susceptible to interference and are honed to represent new 'how to' knowledge (Karni, 1996; Karni and Bertini, 1997; Dudai et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on memory consolidation.

claim: Memory consolidation is the process by which memories become less susceptible to interference and are honed to represent new 'how to' knowledge.
source: These latter, delayed gains emerging in the post learning interval are believed to reflect memory consolidation—the process by which memories become less susceptible to interference and are honed to represent new 'how to' knowledge (Karni, 1996; Karni and Bertini, 1997; Dudai et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research defining memory consolidation.

claim: Offline gains can be sleep-dependent.
source: Offline gains can be sleep-dependent (Stickgold, 2005; Karni et al., 1994), but can occur also after a wakefulness period (Roth et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Offline gains can occur after a wakefulness period.
source: Offline gains can be sleep-dependent (Stickgold, 2005; Karni et al., 1994), but can occur also after a wakefulness period (Roth et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Sleep-dependent consolidation may play a role in the observed offline gains.
source: Since our protocol included a sleep interval, sleep-dependent consolidation may play a role, but future studies using polysomnography to relate sleep parameters with offline gains would be needed to resolve this question.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential role of sleep.

claim: The results indicate the existence of a post-session memory consolidation phase in incidental category learning within which category knowledge is elaborated to a degree that it can be expressed in subsequent performance, even if it was not apparent by the end of the learning session.
source: At present, the results indicate the existence of a post-session memory consolidation phase in incidental category learning within which category knowledge is elaborated to a degree that it can be expressed in subsequent performance, even if it was not apparent by the end of the learning session.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the pattern of results showing emergence of RT Costs on Day-2 in Exp 2.

claim: The many-to-one correspondence of category exemplars and visuomotor task demands may have been instrumental in prompting different learning trajectories.
source: The many-to-one correspondence of category exemplars and visuomotor task demands may have been instrumental in prompting these different learning trajectories.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the mechanism underlying differential learning.

claim: A change in the way that within-category exemplar variability was experienced (across or within trials) had a profound influence on the course of incidental learning.
source: Overall, a change in the way that within-category exemplar variability was experienced (across or within trials) had a profound influence on the course of incidental learning.
evidence: This claim is supported by the differential learning outcomes between Exp 2 and Exp 3.

claim: A tighter coupling of exemplar variability to visuomotor task demands (Exp 3) proved advantageous in early learning.
source: A tighter coupling of exemplar variability to visuomotor task demands (Exp 3) proved advantageous in early learning, but ultimately did not confer a benefit to long-term retention and generalization at the final session.
evidence: This claim is supported by the Day-1 RT Cost in Exp 3 and equivalent Day-10 generalization across experiments.

claim: Tighter coupling of exemplar variability to visuomotor task demands ultimately did not confer a benefit to long-term retention and generalization at the final session.
source: A tighter coupling of exemplar variability to visuomotor task demands (Exp 3) proved advantageous in early learning, but ultimately did not confer a benefit to long-term retention and generalization at the final session.
evidence: This claim is supported by the equivalent Day-10 RT Costs and generalization performance across experiments.

claim: Better within-session (online) learning may not necessarily lead to better retention across longer time periods.
source: This pattern of results is resonant with the notion that better within-session (online) learning may not necessarily lead to better retention across longer time periods (Bjork and Bjork, 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research and the current experimental findings.

claim: Poor online learners show greater overnight consolidation of auditory regularities.
source: and with previous research reporting greater overnight consolidation of auditory regularities among poor online learners (Ballan et al., 2023)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Difficult auditory regularities are more likely to be consolidated if a night of sleep is afforded.
source: as well as reports that difficult auditory regularities are more likely to be consolidated if a night of sleep is afforded (Durrant et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Participants' early learning in the first session was predictive of learning evident in subsequent sessions.
source: Nonetheless, we observe that participants' early learning in the first session was predictive of learning evident in subsequent sessions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analyses showing relationships between RT Costs across sessions.

claim: What is consolidated and retained in the long run appears to constitute category knowledge rather than a lasting mnemonic trace of the specific sound exemplars that were actually encountered.
source: Importantly, what is consolidated and retained in the long run appears to constitute category knowledge rather than a lasting mnemonic trace of the specific sound exemplars that were actually encountered, since learners were able to generalize to novel exemplars nine days after the initial learning experience.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the generalization to novel exemplars on Day-10.

claim: The RT Cost was absent when sounds provided no category-to-visual target regularity.
source: Prior studies of incidental learning in the SMART task found that the RT Cost was absent when sounds provided no category-to-visual target regularity (Gabay et al., 2023)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The RT Cost was absent when sounds deterministically mapped to targets, but not in a manner that preserved underlying category regularities.
source: or when sounds deterministically mapped to targets, but not in a manner that preserved underlying category regularities (Gabay et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: RT Costs were absent when novel category-consistent exemplars were introduced in the SMART.
source: RT Costs were also absent when novel category-consistent exemplars were introduced in the SMART (Gabay et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The findings point to the development of category knowledge that extends beyond auditory-visual-motor associations.
source: Collectively, these findings point to the development of category knowledge that extends beyond auditory-visual-motor associations; the findings cannot be explained by a non-specific cost to performance resulting from a change in the auditory environment.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the pattern of results across studies.

claim: The findings cannot be explained by a non-specific cost to performance resulting from a change in the auditory environment.
source: Collectively, these findings point to the development of category knowledge that extends beyond auditory-visual-motor associations; the findings cannot be explained by a non-specific cost to performance resulting from a change in the auditory environment.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the specificity of RT Costs to category-preserving conditions.

claim: Category learning does not reliably occur across passive observation of the auditory-visual patterns in the SMART task.
source: Relatedly, prior studies make clear that category learning does not reliably occur across passive observation of the auditory-visual patterns in the SMART task, or when participants make a category-nonspecific, generic motor response to report simply the presence of a visual target.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from prior research findings.

claim: Category learning does not reliably occur when participants make a category-nonspecific, generic motor response to report simply the presence of a visual target.
source: Relatedly, prior studies make clear that category learning does not reliably occur across passive observation of the auditory-visual patterns in the SMART task, or when participants make a category-nonspecific, generic motor response to report simply the presence of a visual target.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from prior research findings.

claim: The relationship of auditory regularities defining a category to distinct visuomotor task demands appears to be the 'representational glue' that binds distinct exemplars together to develop category knowledge that generalizes to novel exemplars consistent with the category regularities.
source: Instead, the relationship of auditory regularities defining a category to distinct visuomotor task demands appears to be the 'representational glue' that binds distinct exemplars together to develop category knowledge that generalizes to novel exemplars consistent with the category regularities (Gabay et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the pattern of results and supported by citation.

claim: RT facilitation in the SMART task may capture both the development of auditory category knowledge and more general skills such as the visual stimulus-response mapping.
source: RT facilitation in the SMART task may capture both the development of auditory category knowledge and more general skills such as the visual stimulus-response mapping.
evidence: This is an inference about the composite nature of RT facilitation.

claim: The RT Cost is elicited only with some level of category knowledge.
source: Importantly, the RT Cost is elicited only with some level of category knowledge.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the logic of the RT Cost measure.

claim: Category reactivation across the SMART task may have influenced generalization assessed in the final session.
source: Despite its advantages, this approach leaves open the possibility that category reactivation across the SMART task may have influenced generalization assessed in the final session.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about a potential confound.

claim: The nature of the category regularity associated with the visuomotor target had an influence on learning in Exp 3.
source: The nature of the category regularity associated with the visuomotor target had an influence on learning, at least in Exp 3 where post-test categorization was more accurate for unidimensional, compared to multidimensional, categories.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing differential accuracy.

claim: Post-test categorization was more accurate for unidimensional, compared to multidimensional, categories in Exp 3.
source: The nature of the category regularity associated with the visuomotor target had an influence on learning, at least in Exp 3 where post-test categorization was more accurate for unidimensional, compared to multidimensional, categories.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The finding of more accurate unidimensional category learning is consistent with prior research under single-session incidental training conditions.
source: This is consistent with prior research (Gabay et al., 2015) under single-session incidental training conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: There is a complex relationship between how categories are defined by a single, or multiple, input dimensions, and whether the distributions defining the categories are deterministic or probabilistic in their sampling, and whether training is incidental or driven by overt feedback.
source: It has been suggested that there is a complex relationship between how categories are defined by a single, or multiple, input dimensions, and whether the distributions defining the categories are deterministic (as they were here) or probabilistic in their sampling on the one hand, and whether training is incidental or driven by overt feedback on the other (Roark and Holt, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: An advantage for unidimensional category learning in incidental training may relate to the affordance of being more easily verbalizable.
source: It will be important for future research to assess whether – as in visual category learning under overt training conditions (Ashby and Maddox, 2005) – an advantage for unidimensional category learning in incidental training relates to the affordance of being more easily verbalizable.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about a potential mechanism, supported by citation.

claim: The observation of offline learning gains even for the simple visuomotor task without auditory stimuli in Exp 1 makes the case that we must be attentive to how even the simplest task demands can trigger task-specific learning that may masquerade as other forms of learning.
source: The observation of offline learning gains even for the simple visuomotor task without auditory stimuli in Exp 1 makes the case that we must be attentive to how even the simplest task demands can trigger task-specific learning that may masquerade as other forms of learning.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the Exp 1 results showing offline gains without sounds.

claim: The robust facilitation of RT across sessions appears to be largely driven by robust post-session, consolidation phase changes in the execution of the visuomotor task—visuomotor learning unrelated to the availability of an auditory input.
source: Without Exp 1 as a baseline, it would be easy to attribute the robust facilitation of RT across sessions to auditory category learning. Instead, this facilitation appears to be largely driven by robust post-session, consolidation phase changes in the execution of the visuomotor task—visuomotor learning unrelated to the availability of an auditory input.
evidence: This claim is inferred from comparison of Exp 1 with Exp 2 and Exp 3.

claim: There is no relationship between the RT facilitation across sessions and category generalization in the final session in Exp 2 and 3.
source: This can explain the finding of no relationship between the RT facilitation across sessions and category generalization in the final session in Exp 2 and 3.
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analyses showing no relationship.

claim: Incidental auditory category learning and visuomotor learning may interact, so that overall SMART performance is constrained under conditions of more challenging auditory category learning.
source: This leaves open the possibility that incidental auditory category learning and visuomotor learning may interact, so that overall SMART performance is constrained under conditions of more challenging auditory category learning.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential interaction effects.

claim: In the context of the more difficult category learning challenge afforded in Exp 2, the offline gains evident in RT facilitation between-sessions were smaller than those observed in either the purely visuomotor task of Exp 1 or the less challenging auditory category learning of Exp 3.
source: In the context of the more difficult category learning challenge afforded in Exp 2, the offline gains evident in RT facilitation between-sessions were smaller than those observed in either the purely visuomotor task of Exp 1 or the less challenging auditory category learning of Exp 3.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of offline gains across experiments.

claim: Understanding how organisms come to treat physically distinct objects that share deeper statistical structure as functionally equivalent is central to understanding cognition.
source: Understanding how organisms come to treat physically distinct objects that share deeper statistical structure as functionally equivalent is central to understanding cognition.
evidence: This is a general statement about the importance of category learning that draws from established scientific understanding.

claim: Most of what we know about category learning has come from studies examining learning under explicit training with overt feedback.
source: Yet, most of what we know about category learning has come from studies examining learning under explicit training with overt feedback.
evidence: This is a general statement about the state of the field that draws from established knowledge.

claim: Incidental learning continues to evolve after the learning experience has ended.
source: Our results show that incidental learning continues to evolve after the learning experience has ended, i.e., in the interval following the learning-training session.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental findings showing offline gains.

claim: Brief, incidental experience with novel sound categories that align with a very simple visuomotor task led young adult participants to capitalize on the presence of auditory stimuli to support visuomotor task performance.
source: Brief, incidental experience with novel sound categories that align with a very simple visuomotor task led young adult participants to capitalize on the presence of auditory stimuli, despite the lack of a simple stimulus-response association, to support visuomotor task performance.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental findings showing RT Costs.

claim: The learning process initiated in the session continues in the post-session interval resulting in delayed gains in the ability of the learners to subsequently employ the new auditory knowledge in performing the visuomotor task.
source: Our results show clearly that the learning process initiated in the session continues in the post-session interval resulting in delayed gains in the ability of the learners to subsequently employ the new auditory knowledge in performing the visuomotor task.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental findings showing emergence of RT Costs on Day-2.

claim: In capitalizing on the auditory stimuli learners seem to build lasting category representations that support both the long-term retention of the new auditory category knowledge and its generalization to similar, novel sensory experiences nine days later.
source: In capitalizing on the auditory stimuli learners seem to build lasting category representations that support both the long-term retention of the new auditory category knowledge and its generalization to similar, novel sensory experiences nine days later.
evidence: This claim is supported by the Day-10 RT Costs and generalization performance.

claim: The findings are resonant with research in motor and perceptual domains indicating the existence of a consolidation phase in the development of skills.
source: Consistent with prior reports of consolidation phase offline gains for category knowledge (Djonlagic et al., 2009; Maddox et al., 2009; Barsky et al., 2015), our findings are resonant with research in motor (Karni et al., 1998) and perceptual domains (Karni and Sagi, 1993; Durrant et al., 2011; de la Chapelle et al., 2022; López-Barroso et al., 2016) indicating the existence of a consolidation phase in the development of skills (Karni, 1996; Dudai et al., 2015; Stickgold, 2005; Robertson et al., 2004)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The findings extend prior research on consolidation to incidental category learning.
source: and extend these findings to incidental category learning.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the current findings in the context of prior research.

claim: The results may be particularly relevant in understanding speech category learning, which proceeds incidentally without explicit feedback.
source: In this regard, the results may be particularly relevant in understanding speech category learning, which proceeds incidentally without explicit feedback. (Lim and Holt, 2011; Lim et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the relevance of the findings, supported by citations.

claim: Four nonspeech auditory categories are defined across six exemplars.
source: Figure 1A illustrates four novel nonspeech auditory categories, drawn from prior research (Gabay et al., 2015; Leech et al., 2009; Wade and Holt, 2005; Liu and Holt, 2011; Lim et al., 2019; Gabay et al., 2018; Emberson et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by Figure 1A and citations to prior research.

claim: Categories A and B are characterized by a unidimensional acoustic attribute (offset rises or falls).
source: Categories A and B are characterized by a unidimensional acoustic attribute (offset rises or falls)
evidence: This claim is supported by Figure 1A description.

claim: Categories C and D cannot be defined by a single acoustic attribute and instead are multidimensional, with distributional structure in higher-order perception space.
source: whereas Categories C and D cannot be defined by a single acoustic attribute and instead are multidimensional, with distributional structure in higher-order perception space
evidence: This claim is supported by Figure 1A description.

claim: In the SMART task each auditory category uniquely predicts the upcoming location of a visual target.
source: In the Systematic Multimodal Association Reaction Time (SMART) task each auditory category uniquely predicts the upcoming location of a visual target.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Participants respond with a keypress to indicate the visual target location in the SMART task.
source: Participants respond with a keypress to indicate the visual target location.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental procedure shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Each of three experiments involves three behavioral testing sessions (Day 1, Day 2, Day 10).
source: Each of three experiments involves three behavioral testing sessions (Day 1, Day 2, Day 10).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Blocks 7, 10, and 13 destroy the category-to-location relationship through randomization of sounds to locations to examine the impact on visuomotor response as a response time cost.
source: Blocks 7, 10, and 13 destroy this relationship through randomization of sounds to locations to examine the impact on visuomotor response (as a response time cost).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Examination of performance on Day 2 and Day 10 informs offline gains (response time facilitation), consolidation of incidental category learning, and its retention.
source: Examination of performance on Day 2 and Day 10 informs offline gains (response time facilitation), consolidation of incidental category learning, and its retention.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design and analysis approach shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Exp 1 examines visuomotor task demands without auditory exemplars preceding the visual target to characterize putative visuomotor learning, consolidation and retention.
source: Exp 1 examines visuomotor task demands without auditory exemplars preceding the visual target to characterize putative visuomotor learning, consolidation and retention.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Exp 2 examines incidental auditory category learning when, on each trial, a single category exemplar is repeated five times and predicts the upcoming location of the visual target.
source: Exp 2 examines incidental auditory category when, on each trial, a single category exemplar is repeated five times and predicts the upcoming location of the visual target; exemplar variability is experienced across, not within, trials.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In Exp 2, exemplar variability is experienced across, not within, trials.
source: Exp 2 examines incidental auditory category when, on each trial, a single category exemplar is repeated five times and predicts the upcoming location of the visual target; exemplar variability is experienced across, not within, trials.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Exp 3 examines incidental learning when within-category variability is more tightly coupled to visuomotor task demands.
source: Exp 3 examines incidental learning when within-category variability is more tightly coupled to visuomotor task demands; five unique exemplars are sampled from a category on each trial and, as in Exp 2, the category identity predicts the location of the upcoming visual target.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In Exp 3, five unique exemplars are sampled from a category on each trial.
source: Exp 3 examines incidental learning when within-category variability is more tightly coupled to visuomotor task demands; five unique exemplars are sampled from a category on each trial and, as in Exp 2, the category identity predicts the location of the upcoming visual target.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In Exp 3, the category identity predicts the location of the upcoming visual target.
source: Exp 3 examines incidental learning when within-category variability is more tightly coupled to visuomotor task demands; five unique exemplars are sampled from a category on each trial and, as in Exp 2, the category identity predicts the location of the upcoming visual target.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design shown in Figure 1C.
